The assumptions are differentiability of \(U\) and Lipschitz continuity of \(\nabla U\). The Riesz isometry identifies

\[DU(x)=\operatorname{Riesz}(\nabla U(x)).\]

Since the Riesz map and the gradient are continuous, \(x\mapsto DU(x)\) is continuous. The criterion contDiff_one_iff_fderiv now yields \(U\in C^1\). Lean rewrites the derivative field by toDual_comp_gradient and composes the two continuous maps. No Hessian or twice-continuously-differentiable potential is assumed.

steps.title: Establish spatial admissibility of the actual Gibbs-relative density
steps.body:
The relative density is \(r_t(y)=Z e^{U(y)}p_t(y)\). The partition factor \(Z\) is constant in space, \(e^U\) is \(C^1\) because \(U\) is \(C^1\), and the actual Gaussian mixture \(p_t\) is \(C^1\). Therefore \(r_t\) is \(C^1\) at every positive time.

The Lean proof follows this product exactly using contDiff_const.mul, the potential theorem followed by exp, and interpolationLebesgueDensity_contDiff. Together with pointwise positivity and normalization from the density-construction module, this discharges the smooth test-class premises of IsLogSobolev.

steps.title: Apply the target LSI directly to the constructed interpolation law
steps.body:
Use the actual positive normalized \(C^1\) relative density as the LSI test. This gives

\[2\alpha\,\mathrm{KL}(\rho_t\mid\nu)\le I(\rho_t\mid\nu).\]

This theorem retains extended nonnegative values, so neither finiteness is silently assumed. Lean obtains the Gibbs probability instance from hLSI.1; hLSI.2 is applied with the already proved positivity, \(C^1\) regularity, and relative probability normalization. Finally tiltedMeasure_interpolationRelativeDensity replaces the induced tilted measure with the actual Gaussian interpolation law. The only functional-inequality hypothesis is the target's LSI.

steps.title: Record the square-norm Jensen inequality for probability measures
steps.body:
For a square-integrable random vector \(F\) under a probability measure, convexity of squared norm gives

\[\left\|\int F\,d\mu\right\|^2\le\int\|F\|^2\,d\mu.\]

Lean obtains convexity by applying ConvexOn.pow to convexity and nonnegativity of the norm, with exponent two. map_integral_le then applies Jensen on the whole vector space. MemLp supplies both integrability of \(F\) and of \(\|F\|^2\). This general lemma is used under the normalized Gaussian posterior at each proposed state.

steps.title: Define Bayes posterior on the initial mixture component
steps.body:
At a fixed proposed point \(y\), let \(p(y)=\int K_a(c(x),y)\,d\mu(x)\). The posterior law of the initial component is

\[\lambda_y(dx)=\frac{K_a(c(x),y)}{p(y)}\,\mu(dx).\]

gaussianPosterior constructs this measure with withDensity. The definition is total, while its intended probability interpretation uses \(a>0\), measurability of the center, and positivity of the mixing probability law. The following lemmas establish positivity of the denominator and normalization explicitly, before using Jensen.

steps.title: Prove the real mixture denominator is everywhere positive
steps.body:
Every component \(K_a(c(x),y)\) is positive because its normalizer and exponential are positive. Its support as a function of \(x\) is therefore the whole initial-state space, which has probability one.

The Lean proof uses integral_pos_iff_support_of_nonneg, with integrability from the common Gaussian peak bound. The local support equality hs converts the condition to positive mass of the whole space. Thus \(p(y)>0\) at every point, allowing Bayes normalization and the logarithmic score to be defined pointwise.

steps.title: Check posterior normalization by cancellation of the actual mixture integral
steps.body:
The total posterior mass equals

\[\int\frac{K_a(c(x),y)}{p(y)}\,d\mu(x)=\frac{p(y)}{p(y)}=1.\]

Lean first records positive denominator hp and integrable kernel hq. The definition of withDensity expresses mass as a nonnegative integral. ofReal_integral_eq_lintegral_ofReal converts it to the ordinary integral, justified by integrability and nonnegativity of the normalized kernel. integral_div pulls out the denominator and div_self hp.ne' performs the normalization.

steps.title: Prove posterior displacement has finite conditional second moment
steps.body:
The posterior may arise from an initial law without moments. Nevertheless, at each fixed \(y\),

\[\int\|y-c(x)\|^2\,d\lambda_y(x)=\frac{1}{p(y)}\int K_a(c(x),y)\|y-c(x)\|^2\,d\mu(x)<\infty.\]

The quadratic Gaussian envelope bounds the numerator's integrand by \(N_a/a\). Lean's integrable_withDensity_iff_integrable_smul' changes posterior integrability into the displayed weighted integral under \(\mu\). The proof hsquare dominates it by the integrable constant \(N_a/(ap(y))\). Measurability follows from the measurable center and absolute continuity of the posterior. The standard \(L^2\) characterization then supplies MemLp for the displacement.

steps.title: Identify the mixture score as the posterior component-score mean
steps.body:
Dividing the mixture derivative by its positive value gives

\[\nabla\log p(y)=-2a\int(y-c(x))\,d\lambda_y(x).\]

Lean differentiates \(\log p\) using the actual mixture derivative and the nonzero denominator. The Riesz inverse commutes with the Bochner integral; hgrad identifies the inverse image of each component derivative with \(-2aK_a(c(x),y)(y-c(x))\). Expanding the posterior via integral_withDensity_eq_integral_toReal_smul gives the same integral divided by \(p(y)\). The final scalar cancellations establish the equality pointwise, rather than merely choosing an almost-everywhere score representative.

steps.title: Use posterior Jensen to bound the pointwise mixture score energy
steps.body:
Applying square-norm Jensen to the posterior score identity yields

\[p(y)\|\nabla\log p(y)\|^2\le4a^2\int K_a(c(x),y)\|y-c(x)\|^2\,d\mu(x).\]

The posterior is a probability measure, and its displacement is square integrable by the preceding lemmas; these are the exact hypotheses needed for Jensen. Lean records that inequality as hj, scales it by \(4a^2p(y)\), expands the posterior integral, and cancels \(p(y)\) using positivity. This gives a usable unnormalized density inequality whose right side can be integrated over the proposed state by Fubini.

steps.title: Compute the exact Gaussian component displacement energy
steps.body:
At precision \(1/(4t)\), the component density is the law of \(c+\sqrt{2t}Z\). Therefore

\[\int K_{1/(4t)}(c,y)\|y-c\|^2\,dy=\mathbb E\|\sqrt{2t}Z\|^2=2td.\]

The proof includes integrability, not only an integral identity. gaussian_proposal_radial_density identifies the normalized density with the actual affine Gaussian law. Gaussian square integrability proves hnoise; integrable_map_measure transfers it to the proposed state, and the density-integrability equivalence gives the weighted Lebesgue integrand. The integral identity then follows from the map formula, \((\sqrt{2t})^2=2t\), and the already proved standard Gaussian moment \(\mathbb E\|Z\|^2=d\).

steps.title: Integrate posterior Jensen to obtain the universal smoothing Fisher bound
steps.body:
Integrate the pointwise score inequality, use Fubini, and insert the component displacement moment:

\[\int p(y)\|\nabla\log p(y)\|^2\,dy\le4\left(\frac1{4t}\right)^2\int2td\,d\mu=\frac d{2t}.\]

Lean first proves joint integrability of the density-weighted displacement energy as hprod, using integrable_prod_iff and the constant component moment. The right side of pointwise Jensen is consequently integrable. Continuity of the mixture score supplies measurability of the left integrand, so Integrable.mono' proves hW. Only after establishing both integrability statements does the proof apply integral_mono, exchange the integrals, and evaluate the Gaussian moment. The bound is independent of the initial distribution's location, density, or state moments.

steps.title: Propagate finite gradient energy without a state second moment
steps.body:
Write

\[ abla U(Y_t)= igl( abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X) igr)+ abla U(X).\]

The first term is in \(L^2\) because Lipschitzness bounds it by \(L\|Y_t-X\|\), and the actual frozen displacement has finite second moment whenever \( abla U(X)\in L^2\). The second term is in \(L^2\) by assumption. Lean uses frozen_gradient_error_energy and the \(L^2\) characterization for the discrepancy, adds the pulled-back initial gradient, and transfers the sum to the output measure with memLp_map_measure_iff. The initial position cancels from the displacement, which is why no \(\mathbb E\|X\|^2\) premise appears.

steps.title: Transfer the smoothing Fisher estimate to the actual update law
steps.body:
The generic mixture Fisher theorem applies with \(c_t(x)=x-t abla U(x)\). Rewriting its integral through \( ho_t=p_t\,dy\) gives

\[ abla\log p_t\in L^2( ho_t),\qquad\int\| abla\log p_t\|^2\,d ho_t\le rac d{2t}.\]

The local identity heq matches the actual density with the generic kernel integral. hf is the generic integrability-and-bound result. The density-law identity and integrable_withDensity_iff_integrable_smul' convert its integrability to the actual law; the integral-with-density formula converts the numerical bound. Pointwise finiteness of the density ensures that real and extended density representations agree.

steps.title: Retain everywhere positivity for the real density
steps.body:
The extended mixture density is positive and finite at every point for \(t>0\). Its real conversion is consequently positive:

\[p_t(y)>0.\]

The proof is exactly ENNReal.toReal_pos, with the two previously proved guards interpolationDensity_pos and interpolationDensity_ne_top. This real positivity witness is used whenever Lean differentiates \(\log p_t\) or rewrites the logarithm of a product.

steps.title: Split the relative score into potential and Lebesgue scores
steps.body:
Since \(r_t=Ze^Up_t\), positivity and finite normalization give

\[\log r_t=\log Z+U+\log p_t,\qquad abla\log r_t= abla U+ abla\log p_t.\]

Lean first proves that the real partition function is positive and finite. The function equality heq follows from Real.log_mul and Real.log_exp. Spatial differentiability of \(p_t\) then justifies the logarithmic derivative; differentiability of \(U\) handles the other summand. The proof differentiates the displayed sum and uses linearity of the Riesz inverse. The normalization constant disappears from the gradient exactly because it is spatially constant.

steps.title: Construct finite relative-score energy from two proved L2 fields
steps.body:
The potential gradient remains in \(L^2(\rho_t)\), while the Gaussian smoothing bound gives \(\nabla\log p_t\in L^2(\rho_t)\). Their sum is therefore in \(L^2\), and the score decomposition identifies it with the actual relative score:

\[\nabla\log r_t\in L^2(\rho_t).\]

Lean obtains continuity of the Lebesgue score from \(C^1\) regularity of its positive density, converts the finite Fisher integral to MemLp, and adds it to memLp_gradient_interpolationLaw. The final function extensionality uses gradient_log_interpolationRelativeDensity pointwise. This is the finite-energy fact used for the bounded logarithmic entropy tests.

steps.title: Prove finite relative Fisher information before taking real values
steps.body:
Square integrability of the actual relative score implies

\[I(\rho_t\mid\nu)=\int\|\nabla\log r_t\|^2\,d\rho_t<\infty.\]

Lean starts from the \(L^2\) score theorem and obtains the integrable squared norm. It unfolds relativeFisher, replaces the tilted measure by the actual interpolation law, and rewrites the nonnegative integral as ENNReal.ofReal of the ordinary energy integral. Such an extended value is finite. This explicit proof prevents later uses of toReal from discarding an infinite Fisher information.

steps.title: Derive finite actual KL from LSI and the constructed finite Fisher energy
steps.body:
At positive time, the constructed density is an admissible LSI test, so \(2\alpha\,\mathrm{KL}(\rho_t\mid\nu)\le I(\rho_t\mid\nu)\). With \(\alpha>0\) and finite Fisher information, the KL divergence must be finite.

Lean uses the target's LSI probability instance, interpolationRelativeFisher_ne_top, and interpolationLaw_logSobolev. If KL were infinity, its product with the positive nonzero factor ENNReal.ofReal (2 * α) would be infinity. The inequality would then force Fisher information to be infinity, contradicting the proved finiteness. No entropy continuity or initial density smoothness is assumed to obtain this positive-time finiteness.

sections.title: Time derivatives and spacetime integrability of the Gaussian mixture
sections.intro: Let \(g_x=\nabla U(x)\), \(c_t(x)=x-tg_x\), \(d=\dim E\), and \(K_t(x,y)=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}\exp(-\|y-c_t(x)\|^2/(4t))\). This module differentiates the actual normalized proposal, constructs \(\dot p_t(y)=\int\partial_tK_t(x,y)\,\mu(dx)\), and proves its local spacetime integrability. The only initial moment used is \(G_0=\int\|g_x\|^2d\mu<\infty\); this is derived from finite initial KL elsewhere.

steps.title: gaussianProposalNormalizer eq rpow
steps.body: The proposal normalizer is defined as the reciprocal of an actual Gaussian integral, not as a free scalar parameter. Gaussian Fourier integration evaluates \(\int e^{-a\|z\|^2}dz=(\pi/a)^{d/2}\) for \(a>0\). Substitute \(a=1/(4t)\), simplify \(\pi/a=4\pi t\), and invert the real power to obtain \(N_t=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}\). Positivity of \(t\) justifies the Gaussian formula and the real-power inversion.

steps.title: hasDerivAt gaussianProposalNormalizer
steps.body: On a neighborhood of \(t>0\), all times remain positive, so the actual normalizer agrees locally with \((4\pi s)^{-d/2}\). The real-power chain rule gives derivative \((-d/2)(4\pi t)^{-d/2-1}(4\pi)\). Use \((4\pi t)^{p-1}=(4\pi t)^p/(4\pi t)\) to rewrite this as \(-dN_t/(2t)\). The local equality heq transfers the derivative back to the normalizer defined by the Gaussian integral.

steps.title: frozenGaussianKernel
steps.body: The real component kernel is \(K_t(x,y)=N_t\exp(-\|y-x+tg_x\|^2/(4t))\). The gradient \(g_x\) is evaluated at the initial state \(x\), and is constant when differentiating in \(t\) or \(y\). Its integral over \(y\) is one at positive time by the previously proved Gaussian proposal normalization.

steps.title: frozenGaussianKernelDot
steps.body: Define the explicit candidate derivative \(\dot K_t=K_t[-d/(2t)+\|y-x\|^2/(4t^2)-\|g_x\|^2/4]\). The dimension term comes from the normalizer; the remaining terms come from differentiating the exponent. In the expanded exponent, the mixed inner-product term is independent of time, which explains its absence from this expression. The following theorem verifies that this formula is the derivative.

steps.title: frozen exponent eq
steps.body: Set \(z=y-x\). The squared-norm identity gives \(\|z+sg_x\|^2=\|z\|^2+2s\langle z,g_x\rangle+s^2\|g_x\|^2\). For \(s\ne0\), division by \(-4s\) yields \(-\|z+sg_x\|^2/(4s)=-\|z\|^2/(4s)-\langle z,g_x\rangle/2-s\|g_x\|^2/4\). The vector identity and scalar denominator cancellation are proved separately in the Lean calculation.

steps.title: hasDerivAt frozenGaussianKernel
steps.body:
Write the expanded exponent as \(-A/s-B-sC\), where \(A=\|y-x\|^2/4\), \(B=\langle y-x,g_x\rangle/2\), and \(C=\|g_x\|^2/4\). Its derivative at positive \(t\) is \(A/t^2-C\). The expansion agrees with the original exponent on a neighborhood avoiding zero, so this is also the derivative of the original expression.

Apply the exponential chain rule and multiply by the actual normalizer. Its derivative contributes \(-dK_t/(2t)\); the exponential derivative contributes \(K_t(A/t^2-C)\). Collecting terms gives exactly frozenGaussianKernelDot. No derivative of \(g_x\), and therefore no Hessian, is taken.

steps.title: norm frozenGaussianKernelDot le
steps.body:
Put \(r=y-x+tg_x\) and \(e=e^{-\|r\|^2/(4t)}\). The triangle inequality and \((a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2\) give \(\|y-x\|^2\le2\|r\|^2+2t^2\|g_x\|^2\). The Gaussian envelope gives \(\|r\|^2e\le4t\), while \(e\le1\). Consequently \(\|y-x\|^2e\le8t+2t^2\|g_x\|^2\).

Bound the absolute value of each derivative-coefficient term by their nonnegative sum, multiply by \(e\), and insert these bounds. The resulting convenient envelope is \(|\dot K_t(x,y)|\le N_t[(d+4)/t+\|g_x\|^2]\). It is uniform in \(y\), and is integrable in the initial variable whenever \(G_0<\infty\). Its purpose is time differentiation under the initial-state integral, rather than output-space integration.

steps.title: gaussianProposalNormalizer measurable
steps.body: The map \((t,z)\mapsto\exp(-(1/(4t))\|z\|^2)\) is jointly measurable. Parameter integration makes its real Gaussian integral measurable, even at parameters where the total integral takes its default value. Taking its reciprocal preserves measurability and gives the actual proposal normalizer. The all-time measurable extension is used only to form measurable parameter integrals; positive-time analysis uses the genuine finite normalization.

steps.title: frozenGaussianKernelDot measurable
steps.body: Lipschitzness makes \(x\mapsto g_x\) continuous and measurable. Combine this with the measurable normalizer and the explicit algebraic formula for \(\dot K_t\). Products, norms, scalar inverses, and exponentials preserve measurability, giving joint measurability in \((t,y,x)\). This is the input needed to integrate out the initial variable while retaining measurable time-space dependence.

steps.title: interpolationLebesgueDensityTimeDerivative
steps.body: Define \(\dot p_t(y)=\int\dot K_t(x,y)\,d\mu(x)\). At this point it is an ordinary parameter integral. The subsequent differentiation theorem proves it is the actual derivative of \(p_t(y)\), and the energy estimates prove its integrability, so no analytic assertion is built into this definition.

steps.title: interpolationLebesgueDensityTimeDerivative measurable
steps.body: The component derivative is jointly measurable in \((t,y,x)\). Its strongly measurable parameter integral over the probability measure \(\mu\) is therefore measurable in \((t,y)\). This gives a single measurable version of \(\dot p\) for spacetime Fubini and the entropy chain rule.

steps.title: hasDerivAt interpolationLebesgueDensity time
steps.body:
Fix \(t>0\). Continuity of \(N_t\) supplies a common neighborhood \(S\) on which \(s>t/2\) and \(N_s<N_t+1\). The pointwise derivative envelope then gives \(|\dot K_s(x,y)|\le(N_t+1)[2(d+4)/t+\|g_x\|^2]\) for every \(s\in S\). This bound is integrable in \(x\) by the initial gradient-energy hypothesis, and the component kernel at \(t\) is integrable because it is bounded by \(N_t\).

The parameter-integral derivative theorem now supplies both integrability of \(\dot K_t(\cdot,y)\) and the derivative of \(\int K_s(x,y)d\mu(x)\). On a positive-time neighborhood this integral equals the real density of the actual interpolation law. The local equality heq transfers the derivative to that density, proving \(\partial_t p_t(y)=\dot p_t(y)\) for every output state. No invertibility of the Euler map or step-size restriction is needed.

steps.title: frozenGaussianKernel eq realGaussianKernel
steps.body: The spatial Fisher calculation uses precision notation \(q_a(c,y)=Z_a^{-1}e^{-a\|y-c\|^2}\). Substitute \(a=1/(4t)\) and \(c=x-tg_x\). The normalizers agree by definition, and \(-a\|y-c\|^2=-\|y-c\|^2/(4t)\). This pointwise identity makes the time and spatial calculations use precisely the same normalized Gaussian kernel.

steps.title: norm frozenGaussianKernelDot le weighted
steps.body: Retain the Gaussian factor instead of replacing it by its supremum. With \(r=y-x+tg_x\), the bound \(\|y-x\|^2\le2\|r\|^2+2t^2\|g_x\|^2\) implies that the absolute derivative coefficient is at most \(d/(2t)+\|r\|^2/(2t^2)+\|g_x\|^2\). Multiplication by \(K_t\ge0\) yields \(|\dot K_t|\le K_t[d/(2t)+\|r\|^2/(2t^2)+\|g_x\|^2]\). Unlike the initial-variable envelope, this bound remains integrable in the output variable.

steps.title: frozenGaussianEnergy
steps.body: Use the common nonnegative envelope \(\mathcal E_t(x,y)=K_t(x,y)(1+\|g_x\|^2+\|y-c_t(x)\|^2)\). Its three terms correspond to Gaussian mass, initial gradient energy, and Gaussian displacement energy. This envelope can dominate the derivative with a time-dependent scalar coefficient and can also be reused in spatial integration by parts.

steps.title: frozenGaussianEnergy nonneg
steps.body: At positive time the actual normalizer and the Gaussian exponential are positive, so \(K_t\ge0\). Every term in \(1+\|g_x\|^2+\|y-c_t(x)\|^2\) is nonnegative. Their product is nonnegative; this identifies its norm with itself in the Fubini integrability proof.

steps.title: frozenGaussianEnergy integral
steps.body: For fixed \(x\), Gaussian normalization gives \(\int K_t(x,y)dy=1\), and the centered Gaussian covariance gives \(\int K_t(x,y)\|y-c_t(x)\|^2dy=2td\). Both integrands are genuinely integrable. The initial gradient factor is constant in \(y\), so its integral is \(\|g_x\|^2\). Expand the common energy into these three integrable terms to obtain \(\int\mathcal E_t(x,y)dy=1+\|g_x\|^2+2td\).

steps.title: integrable frozenGaussianEnergy
steps.body: The common energy is jointly measurable. For every initial \(x\), its output section is integrable by the component energy theorem. Since the energy is nonnegative, the integral of its norm is exactly \(1+\|g_x\|^2+2td\), an integrable function of \(x\) under the probability law \(\mu\). The product integrability criterion therefore proves \(\mathcal E_t\in L^1(\mu\otimes dy)\).

steps.title: integral frozenGaussianEnergy
steps.body: Joint integrability allows Fubini, giving \(\int\mathcal E_t\,d(\mu\otimes dy)=\int(1+\|g_x\|^2+2td)d\mu(x)\). Probability normalization and the definition of \(G_0\) reduce this to \(1+G_0+2td\). The displayed equality supplies a finite quantitative bound, rather than relying on an unspecified integrability witness.

steps.title: gaussianTimeCoefficient
steps.body: Set \(C_t=d/(2t)+1/(2t^2)+1\). It is positive for \(t>0\), and is bounded above on any interval \([a,b]\) with \(a>0\) by \(C_a\). The coefficient is deliberately coarse: only local spacetime integrability, rather than a sharp density-derivative estimate, is needed for the entropy chain rule.

steps.title: norm frozenGaussianKernelDot le energy
steps.body: In the weighted derivative bound, denote the three nonnegative coefficients by \(A=d/(2t)\), \(B=1/(2t^2)\), and \(1\). Each is at most \(C_t=A+B+1\). Therefore \(A+B\|r\|^2+\|g_x\|^2\le C_t(1+\|g_x\|^2+\|r\|^2)\). Multiply by \(K_t\ge0\) to prove \(|\dot K_t|\le C_t\mathcal E_t\).

steps.title: integrable frozenGaussianKernelDot
steps.body: The component time derivative is jointly measurable, and its norm is bounded by \(C_t\mathcal E_t\). The common energy is integrable on \(\mu\otimes dy\), and \(C_t\) is a finite scalar at positive time. Domination therefore proves joint integrability of \(\dot K_t\), which licenses the changes of integration order used in the time weak equation.

steps.title: integrable interpolationLebesgueDensityTimeDerivative
steps.body: Fubini applied to the jointly integrable component derivative first gives \(\dot p_t\in L^1(dy)\). The norm inequality for Bochner integration gives \(|\dot p_t(y)|\le\int|\dot K_t(x,y)|d\mu(x)\). Integrate in \(y\), exchange the two integrals, and dominate by \(C_t\mathcal E_t\). The exact envelope integral yields \(\int|\dot p_t(y)|dy\le C_t(1+G_0+2td)\).

steps.title: integrable interpolationLebesgueDensityTimeDerivative spacetime
steps.body: Joint measurability of \(\dot p\) permits the product integrability criterion on \([a,b]\times E\), where \(a>0\). Every time section is in \(L^1(dy)\). For times in the interval, \(C_t\le C_a\) and \(1+G_0+2td\le1+G_0+2bd\), giving the common finite scalar bound \(\int|\dot p_t|dy\le C_a(1+G_0+2bd)\). The time interval has finite measure, so the section norms are integrable. Hence \(\dot p\in L^1(dt\,dy)\) locally away from zero. If \(a>b\), the restricted time measure is zero and the same argument remains valid.

sections.title: Jointly measurable density and relative score
sections.intro: Spacetime integration requires joint measurability in time and state, rather than measurability separately at each fixed time. This module constructs a single measurable extension of the actual positive-time relative score and proves that it agrees with the gradient used in Fisher information.

steps.title: Integrate a jointly measurable Gaussian kernel
steps.body:
The density is a nonnegative parameter integral \(p_t(y)=\int K_t(x,y)d\mu(x)\). The normalizer, affine center, norm, and exponential are measurable in \((t,y,x)\). The parameterized nonnegative integral is therefore measurable. Passing from the extended integral to its real value preserves measurability. Multiplication by \(Z e^{U(y)}\) gives the joint measurability of \(r_t(y)\).

The definitions cover all real times using Lean’s total real operations; only positive times are used for density and score identities. This avoids defining a different measurable representative for each interval.

steps.title: Measurability of the spatial derivative
steps.body:
The derivative kernel is a continuous linear functional proportional to the inner product with the Gaussian residual:

\[D_yK_t(x,y)[v]=-\frac{K_t(x,y)}{2t}\langle y-x+t\nabla U(x),v\rangle.\]

The inner-product-to-dual map is continuous, so this is jointly strongly measurable as a continuous-linear-map-valued function. Its Bochner integral in \(x\), denoted \(A_t(y)\), remains strongly measurable. At positive times the earlier differentiation theorem identifies \(A_t=D p_t\).

steps.title: One relative-score field for all spacetime integrals
steps.body:
Define

\[\mathcal S(t,y)= abla U(y)+p_t(y)^{-1}\mathcal R^{-1}(A_t(y)),\]

where \(\mathcal R^{-1}\) is the inverse Riesz identification of the continuous dual with the Hilbert space. Continuous scalar multiplication, inversion as a measurable real function, and the previous measurability results make \(\mathcal S\) jointly strongly measurable.

For \(t>0\), \(p_t>0\), so the log chain rule and \(r_t=Z e^U p_t\) give

\[\mathcal S(t,y)= abla U(y)+ abla\log p_t(y)= abla\log r_t(y).\]

Thus the measurable field is the actual relative score wherever it is used. Its auxiliary extension at nonpositive time introduces no analytic premise into the proof.

sections.title: Derive the actual Gaussian weak equation for bounded finite-energy tests
sections.intro: Write \(g(x)= abla U(x)\), \(c_t(x)=x-tg(x)\), and \(K_t(x,y)=N_t e^{-\|y-c_t(x)\|^2/(4t)}\). The spatial flux \(F_{t,x}(y)=K_t(x,y)(g(x)-(y-c_t(x))/(2t))\) has divergence equal to the actual Gaussian kernel time derivative. Global integration by parts therefore gives \(\int\dot p_t\psi=-\int F_{t,x}\cdot abla\psi\,d\mu\,dy\) for every bounded \(C^1\) test with \( abla\psi\in L^2( ho_t)\). This module proves all integrability and boundary-product obligations from finite initial gradient energy and Gaussian second moments. It differentiates no Hessian of \(U\) and assumes no weak equation.

steps.title: Choose the spatial flux with the correct Fokker–Planck sign
steps.body:
The component density evolves under frozen drift \(-g(x)\). Its time derivative is \(\Delta_yK_t+\operatorname{div}_y(K_tg(x))\), so define

\[F_{t,x}(y)=\nabla_yK_t(x,y)+K_t(x,y)g(x)=K_t(x,y)\left(g(x)-\frac{y-c_t(x)}{2t}\right).\]

frozenGaussianFlux is the last expression. Its divergence equals the density's time derivative, while the weak equation consequently carries a minus sign after integration by parts. The frozen gradient \(g(x)\) is constant in the spatial variable \(y\), which avoids differentiating the possibly merely Lipschitz gradient field.

steps.title: Differentiate each coordinate of the flux explicitly
steps.body:
Let \(r=y-c_t(x)\). For a direction \(v\), differentiating the kernel and the affine residual gives

\[D_v\langle F_{t,x}(y),v\rangle=K_t(x,y)\left(\frac{\langle r,v\rangle^2}{4t^2}-\frac{\langle r,v\rangle\langle g(x),v\rangle}{2t}-\frac{\|v\|^2}{2t}\right).\]

The Lean proof constructs the derivative of the affine vector factor as hlin, pairs it with the constant vector \(v\) as hi, and multiplies it by the already certified derivative of the real Gaussian kernel. The function equality heq moves the scalar density outside the inner product. Evaluation of the resulting linear map at \(v\), the inner-product rules, and scalar algebra give exactly the three displayed terms. This identity is valid without assuming the potential has a second derivative.

steps.title: Sum the directional derivatives to obtain a coordinate-free divergence
steps.body:
Sum over an orthonormal basis \((b_i)_{i=1}^d\). Parseval gives \(\sum_i\langle r,b_i\rangle^2=\|r\|^2\), completeness gives \(\sum_i\langle r,b_i\rangle\langle g,b_i\rangle=\langle r,g\rangle\), and \(\sum_i\|b_i\|^2=d\). Thus

\[\operatorname{div}F_{t,x}=K_t\left(-\frac d{2t}+\frac{\|r\|^2}{4t^2}-\frac{\langle r,g\rangle}{2t}\right)=K_t\left(-\frac d{2t}+\frac{\|y-x\|^2}{4t^2}-\frac{\|g\|^2}{4}\right).\]

Lean records the two basis identities as hsq and hcross. The residual equality hres is \(r=y-x+tg\); expanding its squared norm cancels the mixed term. The explicit nonzero-time assumption justifies the denominator algebra. This is the same coefficient as the independently derived kernel time derivative.

steps.title: Transport the actual independent pair to its Gaussian Lebesgue density
steps.body:
The pair \((X,Y_t)\), constructed from independent initial state and standard noise, satisfies

\[\mathcal L(X,Y_t)(dx,dy)=K_t(x,y)\,\mu(dx)\,dy.\]

The theorem ULA.gaussian_proposal_pair_density already proves this transport for a measurable center map. Lean applies it to \(x\mapsto x-t\nabla U(x)\), whose measurability follows from the Lipschitz gradient. It then checks that the real kernel here is exactly the previously normalized proposal density. This identity is essential: it lets the proof establish integrability under a simple independent probability law and transfer the result to the Lebesgue pair integrals needed for integration by parts.

steps.title: Prove flux pairings integrable by transporting two L2 factors
steps.body:
For a continuous scalar field \(\varphi\in L^2(\rho_t)\), the coordinate flux pairing is integrable:

\[\int K_t(x,y)\left|\left\langle g(x)-\frac{y-c_t(x)}{2t},v\right\rangle\varphi(y)\right|\,d\mu(x)\,dy<\infty.\]

Under the independent pair \((X,Z)\), the vector factor becomes \(g(X)-(\sqrt{2t}/(2t))Z\). Both terms are in \(L^2\), by the initial gradient hypothesis and the Gaussian second moment. Pulling back \(\varphi\) through the actual update preserves its \(L^2\) property. Lean's hflux and htest are these two facts; MemLp.mul puts their scalar product in \(L^1\). The pair-law density identity and the density-integrability equivalence then yield the displayed weighted Lebesgue integrability. No unproved decay of the test at infinity is used.

steps.title: Admit the gradient pairing of a C1 finite-energy test
steps.body:
Choose the scalar field \(\varphi(y)=D\psi(y)[v]=\langle\nabla\psi(y),v\rangle\). For \(\psi\in C^1\), this field is continuous. If \(\nabla\psi\in L^2(\rho_t)\), its coordinate pairing is also in \(L^2\).

Lean applies the preceding general flux-pairing theorem. Continuity follows from continuity of the Fréchet derivative of a \(C^1\) function, evaluated at \(v\). The equality inner_gradient_left identifies the coordinate derivative with the inner product, and MemLp.inner_const supplies its square integrability. This establishes the \(F_i\partial_i\psi\) integrability premise of global integration by parts.

steps.title: Control the boundary product from boundedness of the test
steps.body:
A bounded continuous test satisfies \(|\psi|\le M\), hence belongs to \(L^2(\rho_t)\) because \(\rho_t\) is a probability measure. The general flux-pairing result therefore gives integrability of \(\langle F_{t,x}(y),v\rangle\psi(y)\).

Lean installs the actual interpolation probability instance, uses MemLp.of_bound, and applies frozenGaussianFlux_mul_integrable. This is precisely the product \(F_i\psi\) required by the integration-by-parts theorem on the whole Euclidean space. Boundedness and finite-energy flux replace a separate compact-support assumption.

steps.title: Match the divergence to the independently differentiated Gaussian kernel
steps.body:
The explicit time derivative from GaussianTimeDerivative.lean is

\[\dot K_t(x,y)=K_t(x,y)\left(-\frac d{2t}+\frac{\|y-x\|^2}{4t^2}-\frac{\|\nabla U(x)\|^2}{4}\right).\]

The divergence calculation gives exactly this expression. Lean rewrites the sum of coordinate derivatives with sum_fderiv_frozenGaussianFlux, unfolds the independently defined frozenGaussianKernelDot, and matches the real kernel definitions. Thus the time/spatial relation used in the PDE is an equality between actual derivatives, not an asserted Fokker–Planck premise.

steps.title: Dominate each unit-coordinate flux derivative by a quadratic Gaussian energy
steps.body:
For \(\|v\|=1\), Cauchy–Schwarz bounds \(|\langle r,v\rangle|\le\|r\|\) and \(|\langle g,v\rangle|\le\|g\|\). The inequality \(\|r\|\|g\|\le\|r\|^2+\|g\|^2\) then gives

\[\left|D_v\langle F_{t,x},v\rangle\right|\le\left(\frac1{4t^2}+\frac1{2t}\right)K_t(x,y)(1+\|g(x)\|^2+\|r\|^2).\]

Lean records the coordinate, square, and mixed-product bounds as hi, hg, hsq, and hcross. The local hbound applies the triangle inequality to the three derivative terms and dominates their coefficients by the displayed envelope. Multiplication by the nonnegative Gaussian density preserves the bound. Only quadratic energies occur, so no fourth moment of the initial gradient is introduced.

steps.title: Integrate the coordinate derivative envelope under the actual pair measure
steps.body:
The common envelope \(K_t(1+\|g(X)\|^2+\|Y-c_t(X)\|^2)\) is jointly integrable: its integral is \(1+G_0+2td\), where \(G_0=\int\|\nabla U\|^2d\mu\). The preceding pointwise bound therefore proves joint integrability of every unit-coordinate flux derivative.

Lean obtains this envelope from integrable_frozenGaussianEnergy and scales it by the finite time coefficient. To supply measurability, heq rewrites the derivative as its explicit polynomial-Gaussian formula; continuity of the gradient then lets fun_prop prove the required measurability. Integrable.mono' finishes using the coordinate energy bound. These are the actual derivative integrals needed before applying Fubini or integration by parts.

steps.title: Apply global integration by parts after proving all three product integrabilities
steps.body:
For one unit coordinate \(v\), global integration by parts gives

\[\int D_v\langle F_{t,x}(y),v\rangle\,\psi(y)\,d\mu(x)\,dy=-\int\langle F_{t,x}(y),v\rangle D_v\psi(y)\,d\mu(x)\,dy.\]

The proof first constructs all three required integrable products: hDf is the derivative of the flux times the bounded test, hFg is the flux times the finite-energy test derivative, and hFf is the boundary product. Fubini gives the corresponding section integrability for almost every initial state. At each such state, the Gaussian flux coordinate is differentiable and the test is differentiable because it is \(C^1\). Lean applies integral_mul_fderiv_eq_neg_fderiv_mul_of_integrable on the whole space, then integrates the section identity back over the initial law. The theorem's boundary condition is integrability of the actual product, not an unproved pointwise decay statement.

steps.title: Derive the actual weak PDE for every bounded C1 finite-energy test
steps.body:
Sum the coordinate identities over an orthonormal basis. The divergence identity turns the sum on the left into \(\dot K_t\), while completeness of the basis turns the sum on the right into \(\langle F_{t,x},\nabla\psi\rangle\). Fubini then yields

\[\int\dot p_t(y)\psi(y)\,dy=-\int\langle F_{t,x}(y),\nabla\psi(y)\rangle\,d\mu(x)\,dy.\]

Lean calls the coordinate integrands A and B. Their integrability is hA and hB; their integral equality is hEq. The identities hsumA and hsumB perform the two basis sums pointwise. Kernel time-derivative integrability times boundedness of the test gives hDot, which justifies exchanging its initial-state and proposed-state integrals. Finally integral_finsetSum commutes the finite sums and integrals. Every premise has been derived from the explicit Gaussian law, initial gradient energy, and the ordinary bounded finite-energy test conditions.

sections.title: Relative Fisher energy and the sharp frozen-gradient error
sections.intro: Let \( ho_t\) be the actual frozen Gaussian interpolation, \(r_t=d ho_t/d u\), \(s_t= abla\log r_t\), and \(G_0=\mathbb E_\mu\| abla U\|^2\). This module proves \(I_t\le4(1+L^2t^2)G_0+8tdL^2+d/t\), local spacetime integrability of the weighted relative-score energy, and the exact pair-law error bound \(\mathbb E\| abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X)\|^2\le L^2(t^2G_0+2td)\). These estimates provide domination for the unbounded entropy test and its truncation limits.

steps.title: norm add sq le two
steps.body: The triangle inequality gives \(\|x+y\|\le\|x\|+\|y\|\). Square both nonnegative sides and use \(2\|x\|\|y\|\le\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2\), which follows from \((\|x\|-\|y\|)^2\ge0\). This proves \(\|x+y\|^2\le2\|x\|^2+2\|y\|^2\), the pointwise estimate used to split relative Fisher energy.

steps.title: interpolationRelativeScoreField energy le
steps.body:
The jointly measurable score field agrees at positive time with the actual relative score. Its decomposition is \(s_t= abla U+ abla\log p_t\). The propagated gradient is square integrable, and Gaussian smoothing gives \(\mathbb E_{ ho_t}\| abla\log p_t\|^2\le d/(2t)\). These facts also prove integrability of the relative-score square.

Apply the squared sum bound pointwise and integrate: \(I_t\le2G_t+2\mathbb E_{ ho_t}\| abla\log p_t\|^2\le2G_t+d/t\). The proof keeps the integrability witnesses for all terms before using integral monotonicity.

steps.title: interpolationRelativeScoreField energy bound

sections.title: Bounded logarithmic tests and their entropy primitives
sections.intro: The unbounded logarithm in entropy production is replaced by a smooth bounded function. The replacement has derivative between zero and one, converges to the identity, and admits an entropy primitive dominated by the actual KL integrand. These properties separately justify the spatial test, the time chain rule, and the limit in the entropy identity.

steps.title: Choose the bounded test and its weight
steps.body:
For a natural number \(m\), write \(c=m+1>0\). Define

\[\chi_m(z)=c\arctan(z/c),\qquad w_m(z)=\frac1{1+(z/c)^2},\qquad\Phi_m(r)=\int_1^r\chi_m(\log u)du.\]

The positive offset in \(c\) prevents division by zero even for \(m=0\). The interval integral is oriented: when \(r<1\), its sign reverses. Lean defines these expressions for every real argument; the entropy claims below explicitly require \(r>0\).

steps.title: Differentiate and bound the test
steps.body:
The arctangent chain rule gives \(\chi_m(0)=0\) and \(\chi_m^{\prime}(z)=w_m(z)\). The denominator is at least one, so \(0\le w_m\le1\). The derivative bound implies that \(\chi_m\) is 1-Lipschitz, hence \(|\chi_m(z)|\le|z|\). Independently, \(|\arctan u|<\pi/2\) gives \(|\chi_m(z)|\le c\pi/2\). This last bound controls the time derivative integrand without any log-integrability requirement. Since arctangent has the sign of its argument, \(\chi_m\) does too.

steps.title: Recover the logarithm and its primitive
steps.body:
As \(m\to\infty\), \(z/(m+1)\to0\). The derivative of arctangent at zero is one; its difference quotient therefore gives \(\chi_m(z)\to z\). At \(z=0\) the claim is exact at every index. Continuity of inversion at the positive denominator one gives \(w_m(z)\to1\).

The function \(u\mapsto\chi_m(\log u)\) is measurable and bounded, hence integrable on every finite interval, including intervals containing zero. When \(r>0\), continuity in a neighborhood of \(r\) and the fundamental theorem of calculus imply \(\Phi_m^{\prime}(r)=\chi_m(\log r)\).

steps.title: Identify the spatial gradient of the test

For a differentiable scalar field \(f\), the Fréchet chain rule gives \(D(\chi_m\circ f)=w_m(f)Df\). Applying the Hilbert-space identification of linear derivatives with gradients yields

sections.title: An integrated chain rule from spacetime integrability

The resulting spatial integral is absolutely continuous and has the integrated derivative almost everywhere. A dominated-limit theorem then passes truncated integral identities to the actual entropy identity.

sections.title: The complete entropy chain rule for the actual Gaussian interpolation
sections.intro:
This module proves the entropy identity and positive-time absolute continuity for the actual frozen-drift Gaussian interpolation. The proof starts with bounded smooth log tests, applies the global Gaussian weak equation and a spacetime \(L^1\) time chain rule, then removes both spatial and time truncations by dominated convergence. All regularity and integrability needed in these steps are constructed from the original Gaussian update and the initial gradient energy.

Write \(\pi=Z^{-1}e^{-U}dx\), \(\rho_t=\operatorname{Law}(X-t\nabla U(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z_0)\), \(r_t=d\rho_t/d\pi\), and \(S_t=\nabla\log r_t\). Here \(Z_0\) is an independent standard Gaussian. The eventual conclusion is \(H(\rho_b\mid\pi)-H(\rho_a\mid\pi)=\int_a^b q(t)dt\), with the explicit raw Gaussian flux \(q\), for every \(0<a\le b\). This identity proves local absolute continuity and the a.e. derivative; they are not assumed.

steps.title: Removing bounded log weights by dominated convergence
steps.body:
Let \(w_m(z)=[1+(z/(m+1))^2]^{-1}\). For a measurable scalar field \(z\) and an integrable field \(f\),

\[\int w_m(z(x))f(x)\,d\nu(x)\longrightarrow\int f(x)\,d\nu(x).\]

The pointwise limit is \(w_m(z(x))\to1\), proved in boundedLogWeight_tendsto. Each weighted integrand is measurable, because the weight is obtained by division, squaring and inversion of measurable real functions. Furthermore \(0\le w_m\le1\), so \(|w_m(z)f|\le|f|\). The Lean proof invokes dominated convergence with the single integrable majorant hf.norm. This lemma later removes the truncation from the actual Gaussian flux, whose two factors are square integrable.

steps.title: Why the square-integrable flux pairing is integrable
steps.body:
If \(v,s\in L^2(\nu;E)\), then

\[|\langle v,s\rangle|\le\|v\|\|s\|,\qquad \|v\|\|s\|\in L^1(\nu).\]

The second assertion follows from Hölder's inequality with exponents \(2,2,1\). In Lean, hf.norm.mul hg.norm supplies membership of the norm product in \(L^1\); memLp_one_iff_integrable converts it to ordinary integrability without assuming that the ambient measure is finite. The measurable inner product is then dominated by this product using norm_inner_le_norm. This establishes actual integrability rather than relying on the default value of an undefined Bochner integral.

steps.title: The real Gibbs density and its normalization
steps.body:
Write \(Z=\int e^{-U(x)}\,dx\), and let \(\pi\) be the normalized Gibbs law. Define

\[J(y)=Z^{-1}e^{-U(y)}.\]

The existing probability-mass argument proves \(0<Z<\infty\); differentiability makes \(U\) measurable and gives strict positivity of the partition function. Consequently \(J(y)>0\) at every point. The measure identity is

\[\pi(dy)=J(y)\,dy.\]

The formal representation of \(\pi\) is initially an extended scalar multiple of volume.withDensity. withDensity_smul absorbs that scalar into the density. The conversion ENNReal.ofReal_toReal is justified by finite nonzero normalization, so the real formula agrees exactly with the original measure. These declarations introduce no strong-convexity assumption.

steps.title: The time derivative of the weighted entropy primitive
steps.body:
Let \(p_t\) be the actual Lebesgue density of the frozen Gaussian update, and let \(r_t=p_t/J\) be its relative density. For the bounded entropy primitive \(\Phi_m\), one has \(\Phi_m'(r)=\chi_m(\log r)\) for \(r>0\). At every positive time, the actual kernel differentiation theorem gives \(\partial_t p_t=\dot p_t\), hence

\[\partial_t r_t=Ze^{U}\dot p_t,\qquad \partial_t[J\Phi_m(r_t)]=\chi_m(\log r_t)\dot p_t.\]

The Lean proof applies the time chain rule first to the constant multiple defining \(r_t\), then to boundedEntropy_hasDerivAt, then to multiplication by \(J\). The remaining coefficient cancels because \(J(y)Ze^{U(y)}=1\), using the inverse of the strictly positive real partition function and \(e^{-U}e^U=1\). This cancellation is what permits the spacetime estimate to use the Lebesgue \(L^1\) bound on \(\dot p_t\).

steps.title: Identifying finite entropy through the chosen density
steps.body:
Suppose \(\mu=r u\) is a probability measure, \(r\ge0\) is measurable, and \(H(\mu\mid u)<\infty\). Then

\[\mathrm{kl}(r)=r\log r+1-r\in L^1( u),\qquad \int\mathrm{kl}(r)\,d u=H(\mu\mid u).\]

Mathlib expresses KL using the Radon–Nikodym derivative. The equality Measure.rnDeriv_withDensity identifies that derivative almost everywhere with ENNReal.ofReal ∘ r. Nonnegativity of \(r\) makes its real part exactly \(r\). Finite KL yields integrability of the log-likelihood ratio, which the KL library converts to integrability of klFun of the derivative. An almost-everywhere change of representative gives both displayed conclusions for the chosen density itself.

steps.title: Integrability of every actual bounded entropy
steps.body:
At \(t>0\), the actual interpolation has a positive \(C^1\) relative density \(r_t\). Its Fisher information is finite from the initial score moment and Gaussian smoothing; LSI then gives finite actual KL. The bounded primitive satisfies

\[0\le\Phi_m(r_t(y))\le\mathrm{kl}(r_t(y)).\]

The preceding density lemma proves that the right-hand side is integrable. The left-hand side is measurable: continuity of \(r_t\) and the derivative of \(\Phi_m\) at positive arguments give continuity of their composition. The Lean mono' argument therefore derives integrability for each truncation from a verified KL majorant. Initial density differentiability, initial Fisher information and a second moment of the state are not required.

steps.title: Convergence of bounded entropy to actual KL
steps.body:
For every fixed positive time,

\[\int\Phi_m(r_t)\,d\pi\longrightarrow H(\rho_t\mid\pi).\]

Pointwise convergence \(\Phi_m(r)\to\mathrm{kl}(r)\) holds for \(r>0\). The domination \(0\le\Phi_m(r_t)\le\mathrm{kl}(r_t)\), together with integrability proved above, gives dominated convergence under the fixed Gibbs measure. Before taking the limit, Lean identifies the integral of klFun r_t with the actual KL through tiltedMeasure_interpolationRelativeDensity. Thus the limiting quantity is the KL of the actual Gaussian law, rather than an independently specified entropy path.

steps.title: The bounded entropy and its time flux
steps.body:
The two functions used in the time integration are

\[H_m(t)=\int\Phi_m(r_t(y))\,d\pi(y),\qquad q_m(t)=\int\chi_m(\log r_t(y))\dot p_t(y)\,dy.\]

Their different measures match the exact cancellation in the weighted chain rule. The definitions are explicit functions of the actual mixture density and its actual kernel time derivative.

steps.title: Admissibility of the actual bounded log test
steps.body:
The spatial weak test is \(\psi_m(y)=\chi_m(\log r_t(y))\). Positivity and \(C^1\) regularity of \(r_t\), combined with smoothness of \(\chi_m\), show that \(\psi_m\in C^1\). Its uniform bound is

\[|\psi_m(y)|\le(m+1)\pi/2.\]

The spatial chain rule gives

\[ abla\psi_m(y)=w_m(\log r_t(y)) abla\log r_t(y),\qquad \| abla\psi_m(y)\|\le\| abla\log r_t(y)\|.\]

The relative score is already in \(L^2( ho_t)\). Its norm domination therefore proves square integrability of the test gradient via MemLp.of_le. Lean explicitly constructs measurability of that gradient from its continuous Fréchet derivative. These are precisely the three hypotheses of the global Gaussian weak equation: a bounded \(C^1\) test and an \(L^2\) gradient.

steps.title: The bounded entropy flux is the actual spatial flux
steps.body:
Let \(K_t(x,y)\) be the Gaussian transition density, \(g=\nabla U\), and \(S_t=\nabla\log r_t\). The proved Gaussian weak equation, applied to the admissible test above, gives

\[q_m(t)=-\iint K_t(x,y)w_m(\log r_t(y))\left\langle g(x)-\frac{y-x+tg(x)}{2t},S_t(y)\right\rangle\,\mu(dx)\,dy.\]

The underlying flux is \(K_t[g(x)-(y-x+tg(x))/(2t)]\). Its divergence equals the actual kernel time derivative; global integration by parts is justified by the previously proved finite-gradient-energy estimates. The code substitutes the test-gradient chain rule and the equality between the explicit measurable score field and the actual relative score. The remaining rearrangement is bilinearity of the inner product and scalar multiplication.

steps.title: The bounded time chain rule without a spatial time-majorant
steps.body:
On any \(0<a\le b\), the weighted primitive has derivative \(\chi_m(\log r_t)\dot p_t\). The kernel theorem proves \(\dot p\in L^1([a,b]\times E)\), while \(\chi_m\) is bounded by \((m+1)\pi/2\). Thus the derivative of the weighted primitive is jointly integrable.

Integrability at time \(a\) follows from the bounded-entropy lemma after rewriting Gibbs measure as \(J(y)dy\). The generic spacetime FTC/Fubini theorem then yields

\[H_m(b)-H_m(a)=\int_a^b q_m(t)\,dt.\]

Applying the same identity on every subinterval proves absolute continuity of \(H_m\); Lebesgue differentiation gives \(H_m'(t)=q_m(t)\) almost everywhere. In code, hdot is obtained by multiplying the actual spacetime \(L^1\) derivative by a bounded measurable function, hderiv supplies the pointwise chain rule, and hweight changes the integrated weighted primitive back to \(H_m\). No common bound on all time derivatives by a single spatial function is assumed.

steps.title: Expressing the flux on one independent probability space
steps.body:
Take \(X\sim\mu\) and \(Z\sim N(0,I)\) independently, and set \(Y_t=X-tg(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z\). Define

\[V_t(X,Z)=g(X)-\frac{\sqrt{2t}}{2t}Z,\qquad \widehat S_t(X,Z)=S_t(Y_t),\qquad q(t)=-\mathbb E\langle V_t,\widehat S_t\rangle.\]

The three Lean definitions give exactly these fields and the raw entropy flux. A fixed product probability space is used at every time, which makes joint measurability and time dominated convergence explicit. The field \(V_t\) is the frozen Gaussian spatial flux divided by its transition density after substituting the actual update.

steps.title: Square integrability of the two actual Gaussian factors
steps.body:
The initial gradient belongs to \(L^2(\mu)\), and the standard Gaussian noise belongs to \(L^2\). Pulling both to the independent product space and taking their scalar combination proves \(V_t\in L^2(\mu\otimes\gamma)\). The actual relative score belongs to \(L^2(\rho_t)\). Since \(\rho_t\) is the pushforward of \(\mu\otimes\gamma\) by \(Y_t\), the measurable-map characterization of \(L^2\) gives

\[\widehat S_t=S_t\circ Y_t\in L^2(\mu\otimes\gamma).\]
